days.title: Prokaryotic vs Eukaryotic Cells
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Distinguish prokaryotic from eukaryotic cells.
  • Identify key structural differences.
  • Give examples of each cell type.
  • Explain evolutionary significance.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Prokaryote — a cell without a membrane-bound nucleus.
  • Eukaryote — a cell with a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
  • Nucleoid — the region in prokaryotes where DNA is concentrated.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Defining Features

FeatureProkaryoteEukaryote
NucleusAbsent (nucleoid)Present
Membrane-bound organellesAbsentPresent
Ribosomes70S80S
Cell size1–5 µm10–100 µm
DNACircular, nakedLinear, histone-bound
Cell wallPeptidoglycan (bacteria)Cellulose (plants), chitin (fungi)

B. Examples

  • Prokaryotes: Bacteria (E. coli), Archaea
  • Eukaryotes: Plants, animals, fungi, protists

C. Evolutionary Significance

Prokaryotes appeared ~3.5 billion years ago; eukaryotes ~1.5 billion years ago. The endosymbiotic theory explains how eukaryotes arose from prokaryotes engulfing smaller prokaryotes.

scenarios.text: A cell has no membrane-bound nucleus.
A cell has mitochondria and ER.
A bacterium.
A cell with linear chromosomes bound to histones.
An organism with a nucleoid region.
A plant leaf cell.

questions.text: Which structure is present in eukaryotic cells but absent in prokaryotic cells?
What type of ribosomes do prokaryotes have?
Which of the following is a prokaryote?

takeaways: Prokaryotes lack a membrane-bound nucleus; eukaryotes have one.
Prokaryotic DNA is circular and naked; eukaryotic DNA is linear and histone-bound.
Endosymbiotic theory explains the origin of eukaryotic organelles.

days.title: Plant vs Animal Cells
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Compare plant and animal cell structures.
  • Identify structures unique to each.
  • Relate structure to function.
  • Explain why certain organelles are more abundant in specific cells.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Cell wall — rigid outer layer in plant cells (cellulose).
  • Central vacuole — large water-storage organelle in plants.
  • Chloroplast — site of photosynthesis in plants.
  • Centriole — aids in cell division in animals.

📚 Lesson Content

Structures Unique to Plant Cells

  • Cell wall — cellulose; provides support and shape
  • Chloroplasts — photosynthesis
  • Central vacuole — stores water; maintains turgor pressure
  • Plasmodesmata — channels between plant cells

Structures Unique to Animal Cells

  • Centrioles — organize spindle fibers during cell division
  • Lysosomes — abundant in animal cells (plants have fewer)
  • Flagella/cilia — movement (some animal cells)

Structures in BOTH

  • Plasma membrane, nucleus, mitochondria, ER, Golgi, ribosomes, cytoskeleton

scenarios.text: A cell has a large central vacuole and chloroplasts.
A cell has centrioles for spindle fiber formation.
A cell has a plasma membrane and nucleus.
A cell has a rigid cell wall.
A cell has mitochondria.
A cell contains plasmodesmata.

questions.text: Which of the following is found ONLY in plant cells?
Which organelle helps organize spindle fibers during animal cell division?
What is the main function of the central vacuole in plant cells?

takeaways: Plant cells have a cell wall, chloroplasts, and a central vacuole.
Animal cells have centrioles and abundant lysosomes.
Both cell types share plasma membrane, nucleus, mitochondria, ER, Golgi, and ribosomes.

days.title: Plant & Animal Tissue Types
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Classify the four main animal tissue types.
  • Describe the three main plant tissue systems.
  • Relate tissue structure to function.
  • Locate tissues within the organism.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Tissue — a group of similar cells performing a specific function.
  • Epithelial tissue — covers body surfaces, lines cavities.
  • Connective tissue — binds, supports, protects.
  • Muscle tissue — contracts for movement.
  • Nervous tissue — transmits electrical signals.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Animal Tissues

TypeFunctionLocation
EpithelialCovering, lining, protection, absorptionSkin, intestine lining
ConnectiveBinding, support, transportBone, blood, cartilage, fat
MuscleMovementSkeletal, smooth, cardiac muscle
NervousSignalingBrain, spinal cord, nerves

B. Plant Tissues

SystemTissueFunction
DermalEpidermis, cuticleProtection
GroundParenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchymaPhotosynthesis, support
VascularXylem, phloemTransport

scenarios.text: Lines the inside of the small intestine.
Transmits signals in the brain.
Blood and bone.
Skeletal muscle fibers.
Transports water in plants.
Outer protective layer of a leaf.

questions.text: Which animal tissue covers and lines body surfaces?
Which plant tissue transports water and minerals?
Blood is an example of which tissue type?

takeaways: Animals have four main tissue types: epithelial, connective, muscle, nervous.
Plants have three tissue systems: dermal, ground, vascular.
Structure of each tissue reflects its specific function.

days.title: Cell Modifications & Specialization
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Describe examples of cell modifications.
  • Explain how modifications enable specialized functions.
  • Relate structure to function at the cellular level.
  • Recognize cell modifications in real-world tissues.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Cell modification — a structural change that enables a specialized function.
  • Surface-area-to-volume ratio — the reason cells modify their surfaces.
  • Differentiation — process by which cells become specialized.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Examples of Cell Modifications

CellModificationFunction
Intestinal cellMicrovilliIncrease surface area for absorption
Root hair cellRoot hairs (elongations)Increase surface area for water/mineral absorption
Nerve cellLong axon, dendritesTransmit signals over long distances
Red blood cellBiconcave, no nucleusMaximize O₂ carrying capacity
Sperm cellFlagellumMotility
Guard cellBean-shaped, thick wallsOpen/close stomata

B. Why Modifications?

Cells modify their structure to maximize surface area, minimize diffusion distance, or perform specialized tasks. This is the cellular basis of differentiation.

scenarios.text: An intestinal cell has many tiny projections on its surface.
A root cell has a long, thin extension.
A red blood cell lacks a nucleus.
A nerve cell is very long.
A sperm cell has a tail-like structure.
A pair of bean-shaped cells controls gas exchange on a leaf.

questions.text: Which modification allows sperm cells to swim?
Why do red blood cells lack a nucleus?

takeaways: Cell modifications are structural changes enabling specialized functions.
Increasing surface area is a common modification (microvilli, root hairs).
Some modifications maximize function by losing structures (RBCs lose nuclei).
Differentiation produces specialized cells from unspecialized ones.
